             TEXAS SCOTTISH RITE HOSPITAL FOR CRIPPLED CHILDREN’S
           RESPONSE BRIEF ON PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

          Texas Scottish Rite Hospital for Crippled Children (“TSRH”) files this Response Brief on

Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (“Response Brief”) in accordance with the State Office of

Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”) Order No. 35 issued on September 22, 2026, and respectfully

shows the following:


                                          I.         BACKGROUND


          TSRH is an intervenor in Docket No. 59182. After consolidation of that docket with Docket

No. 59475 on the issue of need, TSRH appeared in and was an intervenor by operation of law in

the merits hearing for Docket No. 59475. TSRH agreed with the arguments advanced on the issue

of need in the consolidated proceeding and adopted in the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”) – that

the Applicants did not establish need on either a reliability or economic basis. This Response Brief

provides support for that conclusion by responding to the Commission’s Order Remanding

Proceeding to SOAH to provide recommendations on preliminary order issue numbers 11 and 13. 1


                                               II.   ARGUMENT


          A. Preliminary Order Issue No. 11 was addressed in the PFD.

          It is less than clear why the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“PUC” or “Commission”)

believed there was no recommendation in the PFD on Preliminary Order Issue No. 11. The PFD

at pages 71 through 100 explains in detail why need was not established for Import Path 2 on the




1
    See Order Remanding Proceeding to SOAH filed in both Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475.

TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                              Page 2
 basis of reliability. 2 According to the PFD at 98: “Applicants failed to show that the Bell County

East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to Sand Lake Projects—Import Path 2—are needed for four separate

reasons.” Those reasons are: (1) no evidence that Import Path 2, by itself, is needed; (2) the

projected loads did not demonstrate a need for Path 2; (3) a failure to show there was sufficient net

generation in central Texas to serve Import Path 2; and (4) there was credible evidence that new

and planned gas generation could reduce or eliminate the need for Import Path 2. Implicit in those

determinations is that Import Path 2 is not needed to meet NERC reliability standards. 3


     B.     The Applicants have failed to establish that Import Path 2 is needed to achieve
a NERC reliability standard.

        Applicants rely on an ERCOT study to establish that Import Path 2 is needed to achieve

reliability under the NERC standard. That reliance is misplaced.


        First, as the PFD discusses, the ERCOT study is based on flawed load assumptions. 4 As a

result, that study cannot support a finding that Import Path 2 is needed to meet a NERC reliability

standard because there is no evidence that taking into account the correct load assumptions that

Paths 1 and 3, which have been approved by the PUC, are insufficient to achieve reliability. In

other words, there is no evidence that Import Path 2 is needed to achieve reliability if the correct

load assumptions are modeled.


        Second, as the Applicants recognize, at least in a roundabout way, even if the load

assumptions are correct, the ERCOT study failed to analyze if the NERC reliability standard could




2
  Docket No. 59475 PFD (Aug. 20, 2026).
3
  PFD at 99.
4
  PFD at 70 to 84.

TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                               Page 3
 be met if the PUC approved Import Path 1, by itself, the PUC approved Import Path 3, by itself,

or Paths 1 and 3 together, meet the NERC reliability standard. In their brief, Applicants note that:


        … the record contains no power-flow study or other technical analysis modeling a
        reliable alternative with those facilities removed [Import Path 2]. 5

        There is simply no evidence in the record to overturn ERCOT's three separate
        independent recommendations, entitled to great weight, that Import Path 2 is
        needed to meet state and federal reliability standards. 6

        The record does not support the ad hoc removal of any component of that plan,
        because no independent analysis or planning study shows that the plan would still
        resolve the identified reliability issues without it.7

        Removing the Import Path 2 Projects within that analysis would introduce an
        untested variable into a complex, multi-year planning and implementation effort
        that would jeopardize the reliability mandate that ERCOT and transmission
        services providers (“TSPs”) are required to meet. 8

        As to the first statement, there is no such study because ERCOT did not do a path-by-path

analysis. Therefore, the study that was done says nothing about whether less than three paths could

satisfy the NERC reliability standard. Stated differently, that three paths will satisfy the standard

does not mean something less would not satisfy the standard.


        The second and third statements that there is no evidence in the record that Import Path 2

is not needed are true but meaningless. There is no need for such evidence because there is no

evidence that Import Path 2 is needed if Paths 1 and 3 have been approved, which they have been.

The Applicants have the burden of proof. It was up to them to show each path is needed. It is not

enough to show all three paths would establish reliability. It was incumbent on the Applicants to

prove that the absence of a path would mean the standard cannot be met. This they did not do.



5
  Applicants’ Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 at 11-12.
6
  Id.
7
  Id.
8

TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                               Page 4
          As to the fourth statement, there is nothing in the record that supports this conclusion, so it

is not surprising that Applicants provide no record citations. If ERCOT had looked at each path

individually in doing its reliability analysis, maybe, maybe, the fourth statement might be true. In

the absence of such analysis, and, therefore, any evidence to support that conclusion, the statement

must be ignored. Moreover, if “Removing the Import Path 2 Projects within that analysis would

introduce an untested variable” the Applicants are admitting that the need for Path 2 is untested

and unproven. 9


       C.      Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 implements PURA § 37.056(d), which applies
only in the event an Applicant sets forth an economic project.

         Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 is not a free-standing inquiry. It comes from PURA §

37.056(d), which directs the Commission to set criteria, “in addition to the criteria described by

Subsection (c),” for granting a certificate “for a transmission project that serves the ERCOT power

region and that is not necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.” Those criteria must

include a comparison of the project’s estimated cost to consumers against the estimated congestion

cost savings for consumers, considering both current and future expected congestion levels. 10 The

Commission must also include findings on those criteria with its decision on any application to

which the subsection applies. 11 By its terms, then, PURA § 37.056(d) is triggered only by a project

that is presented to the Commission as not a reliability project – not when a PFD determines that

the Applicants have not met their burden to establish their chosen basis for justifying need –

reliability.




9
  Applicants’ Brief at 11-12.
10
   PURA § 37.056(d).
11
   Id.

TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                                  Page 5
         The Commission’s own rulemaking history confirms this two-part application structure. In

Senate Bill 1281, the Texas Legislature added the consumer benefits test for evaluating economic

transmission projects. 12 The Commission implemented that basis for justifying need in Project No.

53403, amending 16 TAC § 25.101. 13 The adoption order set out the governing framework plainly:

“A proposed project is classified as either a reliability project or an economic project.”14

(emphasis added).


        The Commission also made clear that it is the applicant who chooses the category, and that

the project is evaluated under the category the applicant chooses. In rejecting the argument that

resiliency should be a separate project category, the Commission explained that “transmission

projects must still be proposed as either reliability or economic projects,” and that “[e]ach of these

project types provides the commission with well understood means of evaluating individual

projects.” 15 (emphasis added). The rule’s text follows the same approach, referring to a project

“that is submitted as an economic or reliability project.” 16 (emphasis added). Under the

Commission’s framework, the applicant’s choice of path decides the need criteria that governs

evaluating the application.


        The PFD recognized and is consistent with this structure. It explained that this was a

reliability project. With respect to Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 the estimated cost to consumers

and any consumer congestion cost savings requests are products of the economic cost-benefit

analysis required for economic projects. 17 Applicants acknowledge that the Commission’s rule

 “distinguish[es] between a reliability project and an economic project and requir[es] congestion

cost savings tests and production cost savings tests for economic projects only.” 18 (emphasis

added).


          The PFD therefore applied the correct framework. Under the Commission’s rule, the

applicant presents its project as either a reliability project or an economic project, and the PFD

properly held Applicants to the project type they chose to present, i.e., a reliability project. In other

words, Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 was fully addressed in the PFD by recognizing that the

project did not trigger the analysis identified.


       D.    Applicants expressly chose to present the project as a reliability project, not
an economic project.

          Applicants built their case on reliability from the outset, not on economics. The Application

presents the project as part of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (“PBRP”). 19 It says the project is

needed to “address reliability issues driven by rapid load growth.” 20 The PFD notes that

“Applicants emphasize that Import Path 2 is not justified on economic criteria but instead is a

reliability project addressing PBRP needs. Applicants underscore ‘reliability projects are expressly

exempt from the economic tests, including the congestion cost savings test.’” 21 Applicants say the

same thing in their remand brief. They state that “a congestion cost savings analysis is not required

for reliability projects,” that “Applicants are not required to demonstrate congestion cost savings,”

and that “[t]he PFD correctly recognized that the congestion cost savings analysis is not required




18

19

TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                                   Page 7
 for reliability projects.” 22 They also endorse the PFD’s statement that Applicants emphasize that

Import Path 2 is not justified on economic criteria but instead is a reliability project. 23


         That choice has consequences under the framework the Commission adopted. Because

every transmission project must be proposed as a reliability or an economic project, Applicants

had to pick one path, and they picked reliability. By doing so, Applicants did not have to perform

and did not perform the economic cost-benefit study that § 25.101 requires for economic projects.

Having presented an application under the parameters for reliability projects, Applicants cannot

now ask for an economic-project finding they never tried to support. Their own concession also

leaves the record without the cost-benefit evidence that Issue No. 13 and § 25.101 call for: an

economic cost-benefit study analyzing the project under a congestion cost savings test and a

production cost savings test.


      E.      The record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings attributable to the
proposed facilities.

         The PFD correctly found that Applicants submitted no evidence estimating the congestion

cost savings from these facilities. 24 Applicants’ remand brief does not fill that gap. It argues only

that the project will provide benefits to consumers “regardless of whether such benefits are

required to demonstrate project need.” 25 The figures it cites are not the analysis PURA § 37.056(d)

and 16 TAC § 25.101 require to address Preliminary Order Issue No. 13. ERCOT’s estimates of

avoided upgrade mileage do not measure congestion cost savings from the Bell County East-to-

Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake facilities at issue. The Independent Market Monitor’s figures



22
   Applicants’ Brief at 3, 16 (quoting PFD at 150).
23
   Id.

TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                                Page 8
 on historical congestion across ERCOT and West Texas show that congestion exists. They do not

estimate how much of these facilities would reduce and at what cost.


       None of this evidence pairs the project’s estimated cost to consumers with a corresponding

estimate of congestion cost savings. It also does not address current and future congestion levels

and the facilities’ ability to reduce them. General statements that consumers will benefit cannot

replace the specific comparison the statute requires. Because that comparison is missing, the only

finding the record supports regarding Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 is the one the PFD made.


       F.     The Commission should adopt the PFD’s resolution of Preliminary Order
Issue No. 13.

       The Commission’s remand asked the ALJs to fully address Preliminary Order Issue No.

13. The Chairman’s memorandum observed that if need is not established on reliability grounds,

the question remains whether need was demonstrated as an economic project. The answer to that

question on this record is no. Applicants never offered the project as an economic project. They

disclaimed any need to show congestion cost savings, and they presented no project-specific

estimate that would let the Commission make the cost-versus-savings comparison PURA requires.

On remand, the ALJs should reaffirm the PFD’s findings that only economic projects require an

analysis of consumer congestion cost savings and that Applicants did not submit evidence

estimating those savings. The ALJs should also make clear that if the project fails as a reliability

project, the record provides no alternative economic basis for granting the certificate.


                                     III.    CONCLUSION


       The PFD answered the remand questions. On Preliminary Order Issue No. 11, the PFD

already found that Applicants never showed that Import Path 2 is needed apart from the other two


TSRH’s Response Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13
PUC Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475                                                              Page 9
 import paths. Applicants never ran a study modeling the grid without it. A plan that was studied

only as a whole cannot prove that one of its parts is necessary. On Preliminary Order Issue No. 13,

the Chairman asked whether Applicants showed need as an economic project if their reliability

case fails. The record answers that question: they did not. Applicants told the ALJs that Import

Path 2 is a reliability project, not an economic project. As a result, the record contains no evidence

quantifying the cost to consumers or any congestion cost savings. Applicants’ reliability case fails,

and having chosen not to apply to have the project treated as economically needed, they offered

no economic case to fall back on (nor could they, given what was in their application). TSRH

therefore respectfully requests that the ALJs issue a supplemental PFD that answers Issue No. 11

in the negative. The supplemental PFD should also find that the record supports no economic

project need under Issue No. 13 and again recommend that the Commission deny the Import Path

2 applications.

          The PFD therefore applied the correct framework. Under the Commission's rule, the

applicant presents its proj ect as either a reliability proj ect or an economic proj ect, and the PFD

properly held Applicants to the project type they chose to present, i. e., a reliability project. In other

words, Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 was fully addressed in the PFD by recognizing that the

project did not trigger the analysis identified.


          D.      Applicants expressly chose to present the project as a reliability project, not
an economic project.

          Applicants built their case on reliability from the outset, not on economics. The Application

presents the project as part of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan ("PBRP").19 It says the project is

needed to "address reliability issues driven by rapid load growth."20 The PFD notes that

"Applicants emphasize that Import Path 2 is not justified on economic criteria but instead is a

reliability project addressing PBRP needs. Applicants underscore 'reliability projects are expressly

exempt from the economic tests, including the congestion cost savings test. „,21 Applicants say the

same thing in their remand brief. They state that "a congestion cost savings analysis is not required

for reliability proj ects," that "Applicants are not required to demonstrate congestion cost savings,"

and that "[tlhe PFD correctly recognized that the congestion cost savings analysis is not required

         That choice has consequences under the framework the Commission adopted. Because

every transmission project must be proposed as a reliability or an economic project, Applicants

had to pick one path, and they picked reliability. By doing so, Applicants did not have to perform

and did not perform the economic cost-benefit study that § 25.101 requires for economic proj ects.

Having presented an application under the parameters for reliability proj ects, Applicants cannot

now ask for an economic-project finding they never tried to support. Their own concession also

leaves the record without the cost-benefit evidence that Issue No. 13 and § 25.101 call for: an

economic cost-benefit study analyzing the proj ect under a congestion cost savings test and a

production cost savings test.


         E.       The record contains no estimate of congestion cost savings attributable to the
proposed facilities.

         The PFD correctly found that Applicants submitted no evidence estimating the congestion

cost savings from these facilities.24 Applicants' remand brief does not fill that gap. It argues only

that the proj ect will provide benefits to consumers "regardless of whether such benefits are

required to demonstrate project need."25 The figures it cites are not the analysis PURA § 37.056(d)

and 16 TAC § 25.101 require to address Preliminary Order Issue No. 13. ERCOT's estimates of

avoided upgrade mileage do not measure congestion cost savings from the Bell County East-to-

Big Hill and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake facilities at issue. The Independent Market Monitor's figures

       None of this evidence pairs the project' s estimated cost to consumers with a corresponding

estimate of congestion cost savings. It also does not address current and future congestion levels

and the facilities' ability to reduce them. General statements that consumers will benefit cannot

       F.     The Commission should adopt the PFD's resolution of Preliminary Order
Issue No. 13.

       The Commission's remand asked the ALJs to fully address Preliminary Order Issue No.

13. The Chairman' s memorandum observed that if need is not established on reliability grounds,

the question remains whether need was demonstrated as an economic proj ect. The answer to that

question on this record is no. Applicants never offered the project as an economic project. They

disclaimed any need to show congestion cost savings, and they presented no project-specific

estimate that would let the Commission make the cost-versus-savings comparison PURA requires.

On remand, the ALJs should reaffirm the PFD's findings that only economic projects require an

analysis of consumer congestion cost savings and that Applicants did not submit evidence

estimating those savings. The ALJs should also make clear that if the project fails as a reliability

project, the record provides no alternative economic basis for granting the certificate.

       The PFD answered the remand questions. On Preliminary Order Issue No. 11, the PFD

already found that Applicants never showed that Import Path 2 is needed apart from the other two
